title_en: World leaders gather for Apec and Asean summits ahead of Trump-Xi-Putin meeting – live updates
excerpt_en: US president flies into Manila amid protests over the Middle East war and the scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica initiative
body_en: Japan proposes Asia oil security task force at Asean Japan ⁠has proposed creating a task force to coordinate cooperation in Asia on oil stockpiling and the release of supplies during emergencies – ⁠one that will allow ⁠neighbours in the region to use idle storage capacity in Japan.
Prime minister Sanae Takaichi told Asean leaders at a summit the initiative would be coordinated with a Philippine-led joint oil stockpiling scheme.
“We intend to promote it as an equivalent of ⁠an Asian version of the International Energy Agency,” she said at the Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) leaders’ meeting.
Takaichi ‌also proposed a Power Gulf ‌Initiative aimed at strengthening cooperation between Middle Eastern oil producers and Asian energy-consuming countries.
The AZEC members are Australia, Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Compared with Japan, Southeast Asian countries hold smaller oil stockpiles, and supplies of crude ‌and petroleum products such as naphtha – a key feedstock for plastics – have become very tight.
China’s Xi Jinping has also met with Vietnam president, Tô Lâm, on the Apec sidelines. We’ll bring you news on this meeting soon.

PNG supports China's 'reunification' of Taiwan Papua ⁠New Guinea’s prime minister, James Marape, ⁠said Taiwan does not operate in ⁠the country any more, during a meeting ⁠with China’s Xi Jinping ‌in Shenzhen.
We hope this assists you in your efforts for reunification... because ‌when Chinese prosper, we all prosper together.”

Marape used the phrase “reunification” – a term used by the Chinese Communist party to frame Taiwan as part of China that must be brought back under Beijing’s control. China has long vowed to annex Taiwan, a self-governing island, using force if necessary.
In response, Xi said China was willing to work with Papua New ⁠Guinea to deepen political mutual trust and continuously take bilateral relations to new ‌heights.
China’s Xi Jinping has met with Papua New Guinea’s prime minister James Marape and comments have been made about Taiwan.

China and Canada agree further tariff cuts: Carney China has agreed ⁠to provide additional tariff relief ⁠for about ⁠C$400m ($280m) in Canadian goods, the ⁠Canadian prime minister’s office said ⁠on Tuesday.
The tariff relief covers ‌C$116 million ‌in exports of ‌frozen pork cuts and C$285 million in fish and seafood exports, Carney’s office said.
Canada and China also agreed to extend by two years ⁠existing remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products, officials said.
We’ll have more on this as it comes to hand.
President Trump will arrive at the Asean and Apec summits in Manila and Shenzhen this week at his weakest moment domestically since the start of his second term.

A year ago, Trump used a similar Asia trip to agree on a trade truce with China and secure investment pledges from Japan and South Korea. This time, Trump is going with his party no longer in control of Congress as of January and with attention beginning to turn to a crop of presidential hopefuls who aim to replace him in 2028.

“I think he, like other presidents, has figured out that in a moment where things are really hard domestically: Get on an airplane and go international,” said Kurt Campbell, a former deputy secretary of state in Joe Biden’s administration.

In 2014 Barack Obama flew to Beijing days after his party lost the Senate to negotiate carbon emission targets with Xi. And in 2006 George W. Bush went to Apec in Vietnam after the Republicans had lost control of Congress.
Some more on Trump suggesting Kim could be a surprise Apec attendee.
Victor Cha, head of the Korea program at Washington’s Center for Strategic and International Studies thinktank, said Trump’s comments suggested he had asked Xi to invite Kim to China.

title_en: RBA board members who voted against rate hike warned of ‘materially sharper downturn’
excerpt_en: Minutes released from latest Reserve Bank meeting as Jim Chalmers says Myefo ‘will cut enough, but not too much’
body_en: Reserve Bank board members who voted against this month’s official interest rate hike were worried about a “materially sharper downturn” in the economy, arguing the RBA should wait to see how higher borrowing costs would hit households.

Minutes from the two-day meeting revealed how three of the nine board members believed it was “prudent to leave more time” to see how the preceding four rate increases would flow through to the economy.
“They also placed somewhat less weight than the other members on the upside risks to inflation and somewhat more weight on the downside risks to economic growth,” the minutes read.
“These members expressed their concern that the economy might be near the point of entering a materially sharper downturn and pointed to the costs in terms of unemployment.”

‘Cut enough, but not too much’ The dissenting view from the RBA’s monetary policy board came as the federal treasurer, Jim Chalmers, promised next month’s mid-year budget update “will cut enough, but not too much”, as he flagged “substantial savings” to help ease price pressures.
Chalmers said savings would be the budget update’s “main focus” amid “intensifying” spending pressures.
“We take seriously and embrace our responsibilities in the fight against inflation,” he said.
Inflation has been above 3% for most of the past five years, eating into Australians’ take-home pay, and is not expected to be back at the central bank’s 2.5% target until mid-2028.
Westpac economists on Tuesday said official figures next Wednesday would show consumer prices jumping to 4.8% in the year to October, from 4.3%, and to the highest since September 2023.

Despite growing concerns among some RBA board members that the central bank may inadvertently push the economy over the edge, the governor, Michele Bullock, on Tuesday said she remained more worried about persistently high inflation than rising unemployment.

In particular, Bullock warned that businesses were starting to treat rapid price rises as the “new normal”, raising the spectre of an increasingly entrenched inflationary mindset that could be difficult to shift without even more damaging rate hikes.
Related: What would tip the Australian economy into a recession we ‘don’t have to have’? | Saul Eslake
“They [businesses] are thinking: ‘You know what? Maybe three [or] 3.5% is the new normal for inflation’,” Bullock told the Australian Securities and Investment Commission forum in Sydney.
“If that gets ingrained … then it’s going to be much harder to bring inflation back down to target.”

Leah Weckert, the Coles chief executive, speaking at the Australian Securities and Investment Commission conference in Sydney, said that cost-conscious families were swapping to cheap protein sources such as mince or eggs, or skipping meat altogether.
“Mince is growing very strongly at every retailer I speak to at the moment, so spaghetti bolognese is alive and well as a family staple,” Weckert said.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The latest evidence of a split on the RBA board comes as Chalmers faces growing pressure to sell the government’s economic strategy to a stressed electorate coming into the summer holiday period.
In a speech at the Asic event, Chalmers said the December mid-year economic and fiscal outlook (Myefo) “will strike some fine balances”.
“It will cut enough, but not too much,” he said.
“It will help ease immediate capacity pressures without putting growth at risk, and make room for the responsible cost-of-living relief we’ve been rolling out without adding to price pressures.”
Amid plunging confidence among mortgaged households, the treasurer pointed to financial markets, which “seem to think rates have now peaked”.
“In contrast, rates are expected to continue climbing in every major advanced economy.”

title_en: Truck driver fired for ‘unsafe’ use of smartglasses in first reported sacking over device in Australia
excerpt_en: Toll employee Ricardo Martins Silva used smartglasses to take photos at an LPG terminal despite the risk of an explosion caused by an electrical spark, a court heard
body_en: A Toll truck driver was fired from work in Victoria after using smartglasses to snap photos at an LPG terminal, in what was described as an “intrinsically unsafe” incident.
It is the first reported case in Australia of a worker dismissed for using smartglasses in a workplace.

The employee, Ricardo Martins Silva, was fired from Toll Transport in July 2025, after eight months with the company as an LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) tanker driver, the federal circuit court heard. His role was to drive a loaded LPG tanker for Origin Energy from the Long Island Point terminal in Hastings, Victoria, for onward delivery.

A federal circuit court judgment last week stated that on 17 June 2025, Martins Silva raised concerns about a truck allocated to him, telling superiors the truck had too much vibration and was jumping excessively.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The judgment stated he was advised to take a different truck, and when he went to the terminal, he took photographs using his smartglasses, and sent them to a superior with a message stating: “I’m going to take the truck back to Dandenong and I’m leaving! There’s no more time for deliveries today!”
The Esso worker at the terminal told Toll that any use of electrical equipment on-site is “intrinsically unsafe” due to the risk of an explosion caused by electrical spark.

Martins Silva was prevented from taking on additional work until an investigation into the incident had been completed, and Origin Energy later asked the employee be removed from work as soon as possible because “his attitude is poor” and “not doing planned deliveries because he is ‘tired and stressed’ is not acceptable”, the judgment read.

Martins Silva sent emails between 17 and 19 June raising concerns about his role, truck allocations and safety issues. The worker on 20 June submitted a complaint about his employment, including safety, and impact of working conditions on his health, among other things.
On 22 June, the employee was advised he was stood down, the judgment stated.
Related: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings

At a meeting on 24 June, what Toll termed as “the glasses incident” was raised with the employee. He was told it was regarded as a “critical safety breach” and that Toll had commenced an investigation process due to its seriousness.

By 30 June, the company decided Martins Silva should be suspended from employment citing, among other reasons, the seriousness of the glasses incident. On 9 July, the employee was informed that taking a photograph with the smartglasses was in breach of Toll’s code of practice, and his contract of employment. His employment was terminated on 18 July, the judgment stated.
Martins Silva claimed the action was in breach of the Fair Work Act, arguing Toll’s actions were as a result of complaints he had made.
The federal circuit court found in the ruling last week that the glasses incident was “on any objective view a serious incident”.

“On the day he wore the smart glasses, Mr Martins Silva was plainly aware of the risks of what he was doing – he went so far as to seek to mitigate the risk by covering his smartglasses with safety glasses,” the ruling from federal circuit justice Karl Blake stated.
“The glasses incident was not concocted or made to look more serious than what it was. It was objectively very serious.”
Related: Privacy watchdog launches investigation into China-based company behind Kmart ‘pervert glasses’ app

Martins Silva had conceded in cross examination that he knew at the time he had done the wrong thing, Blake’s judgment stated, but had written to his employer at the time that his judgment had been affected by the unresolved trauma of a truck fire in which he had been injured in March 2025.

Blake found Martins Silva was not dismissed because he made complaints but “because he wore smartglasses” at the terminal and his employer was of the view that it amounted to a serious safety incident. The application was dismissed.

While the case had focused on safety concerns, since the arrival of Meta’s Ray-Bans and cheaper alternatives such as the Kmart Anko brand glasses, governments have faced pressure to ban the devices over privacy concerns.
Councils across Australia have banned the glasses from some public spaces including gyms and pools, while the federal government is considering bans in government offices.

title_en: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
excerpt_en: The post Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: President Donald Trump announces tariffs at the White House in April 2025. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.
The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.

Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:

The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.
Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.

Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.

But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.

“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.”

The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.

Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries.
“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.”

Gregory Germain, corporate law professor at Syracuse University Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.

That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.

The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year.

The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president, asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.”

Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event.

Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.

“The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference. “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.”

title_en: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
excerpt_en: The post Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Illustration by Matt Rota for ProPublica. Animation by Henrike Lendowski for ProPublica. When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top.

Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children.

Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds.
No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt.

New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show.

According to all four of the major Wall Street credit-rating agencies, New York’s and Los Angeles’ fiscal health make them much better choices for investors. Chicago’s history of questionable borrowing and budgeting — it chose to either ignore or short its pension payments for years — has undermined its credibility.

Its credit rating now sits just two or three levels above junk status, making the cost of borrowing even more onerous. And the city’s chief financial officer, tasked with managing city debt and relationships with credit agencies, resigned last week in stunning fashion, saying she no longer could continue in the role because it would compromise her “integrity and professional obligations.” She had come from Fitch Ratings, a credit agency, and had been on the job for only three months.
Chicago’s Pension Systems Are Less than 50% Funded The city is an outlier among other large cities, where most pensions are at least 75% funded.

Note: Most cities have multiple pension funds. This chart displays the range between the pension fund with the least funding and the most funding within each city. Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number. Source: 2025 city budgets and pension reports (data as of September 2026) Lucas Waldron/ProPublica Options for a financial rescue are limited or unpalatable. Pension obligations, locked in by law and political realities, remain untouchable. There is little public or political appetite to raise property taxes or cut city jobs, particularly among the ranks of police, the city’s largest workforce. A windfall from the city’s still-under-construction casino grows more unlikely than ever.
The office of Mayor Brandon Johnson, who is finishing up his first term in office, blames “reckless financing methods” from past administrations for the city’s financial bind.

“Savings and efficiencies alone cannot solve the city’s persistent structural gap,” the city’s Office of Budget and Management wrote to WTTW and ProPublica in response to questions for this story. In searching for revenue streams, Johnson has sought to impose new taxes on the city’s biggest corporations — an effort that has met stiff resistance.

Tackling the pension crisis, the city since 2023 has paid an additional $1 billion into its four pension funds above what is required by state law, records show, an infusion that the city touts as a stabilizing force.
But, like his predecessors, Johnson continues to rely on borrowing. Since taking office in 2023, Johnson has added $1.9 billion to the city’s debt obligations, according to city data.

That borrowing has “advanced desperately needed investment in economic development and affordable housing in historically underserved communities on the South and West sides,” according to Johnson’s spokesperson.

It also has been used to keep the city functioning. In 2026, for example, Chicago borrowed $166 million to pay firefighters what they were owed for working without a contract — and annual raises — for four years. Officials acknowledged they failed to set enough cash aside annually to cover those widely anticipated costs. The city borrowed an additional $267 million to cover the soaring cost of lawsuits alleging Chicago police officers committed a wide range of misconduct.
In some cases, the Johnson administration has negotiated agreements with its lenders that allow the city to pay only interest for several years, backloading its debt burden.

Chicago’s Debt Payments Were the Largest Category of the City’s Budget in 2026 Note: The aviation budget funds the operation of Chicago’s airports, O’Hare International and Midway International. Source: 2026 Chicago city budget Lucas Waldron/ProPublica With so much of the city budget dedicated to debt and pensions — and more cordoned off by federal and state laws that mandate spending for specific purposes, such as transportation — Chicago officials get to decide how to spend just one-third of its annual budget, records show.

The result for residents: Restaurant inspections are lagging. Complaints about crumbling sidewalks and injuries from those hazards pile up, without timely repairs. The city’s Public Health Department doesn’t have enough caseworkers to handle the intensive intervention needed for children suffering from lead poisoning.

The budget pressures are unrelenting. In August, Johnson announced another borrowing plan to fix a budget shortfall that emerged midyear. He blamed the City Council for overestimating the impact of new revenue streams while his council foes accused him of continuing a pattern of questionable borrowing habits.

title_en: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
excerpt_en: The post Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Matt Rota for ProPublica Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess.
The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble.

The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund.
Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole.

Pension Holiday Snowballs Into Peril In 2000, the city’s pensions were 85% funded, which meant the funds could easily pay benefits to employees as they retired, records show. But a series of decisions in both Chicago and the Illinois capital of Springfield unraveled that strong position, leading to the current mountain of $36.4 billion in pension debt.
First, the twin blows of the “dot-com” bubble bursting in 2000 and the Great Recession in 2007 wiped out nearly $16 billion from those funds.

Around the same time came a self-inflicted blow. In 2005, the state legislature, at the request of then Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, passed legislation allowing the city to contribute less every year than what was actually needed to pay retirees.

As a result, in 2006 and 2007, Daley was able to stop making annual contributions to four pension funds for police officers, firefighters, laborers and municipal employees. He received near-unanimous support from the Chicago City Council. Daley, who was mayor from 1989 through 2011, declined to comment for this story.

Former Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley in 2006 Julio Cortez/AP Daley’s “pension holiday” meant the city could balance its budget without a politically perilous property tax hike. But that maneuver laid the foundation of the current pension crisis facing the city.

In 2010, having seen the financial fallout from the pension legislation, state legislators passed a law that banned city officials from taking another pension holiday by setting a firm schedule for the city to pay back its skipped payments — no excuses allowed.

Two of Chicago’s pension funds must be funded at a 90% level by 2055, with the other two hitting that mark by 2058, according to state law. This requirement caused a spike in the city’s annual payments.
Trying to ease Chicago’s snowballing pension burdens, lawmakers passed a new measure reducing the retirement benefits offered to state employees who began work on or after January 1, 2011.

But that revised law touched off a new set of problems. The well-intentioned effort to reduce costs actually reduced pension benefits too drastically. Under federal law, public sector pension funds must pay workers no less than what they would have earned if they paid into Social Security.
In 2021 and 2025, lawmakers agreed to change the law and ensure that first responders — police and firefighters — in Illinois are paid at least the minimum required by law.

Fixing those funds will cost Chicago an additional $11 billion to get to the 90% funded level required by state law over the next three decades, according to city projections. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the legislation over the objections of city officials.

Long-Term Lease, Long-Lasting Regrets Facing big deficits in 2008 in the wake of the Great Recession, Daley and the City Council found what they thought was a creative solution to the city’s financial woes.

They would lease the city’s parking meters to a conglomerate of investment funds for 75 years in return for $1.5 billion up front. That massive influx of cash meant no one had to make any hard decisions to fill the city’s budget gap and avoid a politically unpopular property tax increase.

A Chicago resident feeds a new parking meter in 2009. The city privatized its parking meters in a $1.1 billion, 75-year deal as a way to get a cash infusion. Charles Rex Arbogast/AP But the deal ended up a loser both politically and financially.

The new owners of the meters immediately jacked up the cost to park, infuriating residents. In a matter of months, members of the City Council began regretting their votes, and Daley announced he would not run for reelection.
By 2025, the city’s meters generated $2.2 billion in revenue for the investors, with another 58 years still left on the lease.

The city considered buying the parking meters back this year, but Mayor Brandon Johnson told reporters “the final purchase price was far too high.” The city would have had to borrow billions to finance the $3.2 billion purchase.
Elected officials across the political spectrum agree that the city would have been much better off raising property taxes instead of leasing the parking meters in 2008.

title_en: Cop31 draft text is attempt to ‘draw out parties’ to find agreement, president of talks says
excerpt_en: Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining
body_en: A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.

Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, said: “It’s a genuine attempt to draw out parties on what they can support and what they can’t. There’ll be things in there that don’t have agreement, but if we only concentrated on the things that do have broad agreement, it would be a very thin document.”

The 18-page draft, which is likely to undergo several more iterations before the scheduled end of the talks on Friday evening, includes among its 144 separate items a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”, and to limit the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris climate agreement.

The document in its current form lays out the competing positions of governments from tiny island states to oil behemoths and emerging economies. It needs ultimate approval by the nearly 200 nations at the UN climate summit.
“We’ve got to start with a broad document, concentrate on getting agreement with some difficult issues, then refine it down over the coming days,” Bowen told the Guardian in an interview.

Alden Mayer, a senior associate at the E3G thinktank, said putting out the draft text at this stage was a gamble. “But it would also be a gamble to wait until later in the week. They have decided to take the ‘full monty’ approach, knowing that many of the 144 paragraphs will not survive the week,” he said. “The question is where does the presidency think the sweet spot is on the various contested issues.”

The wording on fossil fuels echoes a pledge made by all countries at Cop28 in Dubai to “transition away from fossil fuels”, which had no timetable or work programme attached, but is likely to be attacked by oil-producing countries that have hardened their positions since then.

There are also provisions to address the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris agreement and a target to derive 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035, a key priority for the host nation, Turkey.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, called the text “an overgrown garden. There are lots of encouraging green shoots but there are also a lot of weeds that need to be pulled out.”

He welcomed the fleshing out in the draft of a previous promise to triple finance to poor countries to help them adapt to the impacts of extreme weather. “If that language remains in the final version, it would suggest countries are starting to listen to the needs of the vulnerable,” he said.
Related: AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports

The “cover decision” is one part of the expected outcome of this Cop, and some countries – chiefly Russia, Saudi Arabia and the Arab group and some allies – have objected to having one. Cover decisions have been used in most of the 30 previous Cops, taking in resolutions that were difficult to fit into the other formal negotiating strands.
Within the other strands at Cop31, there are still major disagreements among developed and developing countries. Poor nations are unhappy that no new finance is likely to be forthcoming at this Cop.

“Climate action roadmaps without climate finance lead nowhere,” said Siphesihle Mvundla of groundWork, an environmental justice nonprofit in South Africa. “The global south is spending 225 times more repaying debt than they receive in climate finance from the very countries who owe them a climate debt.”

The text contains items likely to be subject to trade-offs among parties. For instance, language calling for “carbon dioxide removal” was attacked by campaigners who see it as a “false solution”, but it is unlikely that some fossil fuel-producing countries would agree any text without such a reference.

Bowen also said fossil fuel-producing countries did not bear more responsibility than consumer countries in tackling the climate crisis. “There are two types of countries in the world, fossil fuel exporters and fossil fuel importers, and we’re all in it together. The idea that everything [is for] fossil fuel exporters is not one I support,” he said. “We’re all part of this process, and just dealing with one and not the other is not realistic.”

He refused to commit Australia, which is one of the world’s biggest producers of coal, to a phaseout of fossil fuel exports, as campaigners and some countries are calling for, but said Australia had a plan to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions and was adjusting for a world in which all countries did the same.

“I accept the logic that all countries will need to reduce emissions, and that means they’re reducing their use of fossil fuels, and that will impact on Australia’s exports, absolutely,” he said. “That’s why we’re preparing our economy for that change.”

title_en: ‘George Michael came out of his coma talking like Jill’: Julia Davis and Rebecca Front on their squirm-inducing comedy Nighty Night
excerpt_en: ‘When Jill and Glen are in bed, that was Steve Coogan’s bed. He was rarely there so we didn’t bother washing the sheets afterwards’
body_en: Julia Davis, creator and star It all started with the character of Jill Tyrell. I’d done Human Remains [a black comedy about oddball couples] with Rob Brydon and was trying to write something of my own. I remembered this woman from Human Remains called Beverley. She was in her 50s, from the West Country and did home hairdressing. She told a client: “The ammonia will burn your ears a bit, Joyce, that’s completely natural.” Bath and Bristol are embedded in my history, so I thought I’d develop that. I made Jill two decades younger and gave her husband Terry cancer, which she uses to her advantage.

I’m drawn to writing about unhappy couples and extreme, cuckoo-in-the-nest women. Nighty Night is like a West Country Fatal Attraction. People I’d met while doing office jobs inspired me. Once I asked to borrow a pen and this woman said: “I don’t feel comfortable with that because you might lose it, so I’m going to say no on this occasion.” I found that rude officiousness bizarre and funny. That fed into Jill. Abigail’s Party and Ingmar Bergman films were influences, and I also loved those 90s thrillers like Single White Female or The Hand That Rocks the Cradle.
Today Jill might be working in cosmetic surgery, botching ops

Those were the glory days of comedy commissioning. I met BBC Three controller Stuart Murphy with one script and did a Jill impression. He went: “Let’s do it.” I cast friends and people I admired: Ruth Jones, Rebecca Front and Kevin Eldon. Poor Kevin, chained to the bed in a nappy.

We needed a romantic male lead – someone like Colin Firth or Greg Wise – so I offered them the role of Cath’s husband Don, the object of Jill’s obsession. They turned it down, obviously. Angus Deayton swooped in and saved the day. Mark Gatiss played Jill’s other love interest, Glen Bulb. He came up with Glen’s twitch himself. We were terrible for corpsing. I met Mark on the worst film ever made, Sex Lives of the Potato Men, and giggled all the way through – partly hysterics due to fear of the script.

Jill’s a sociopath and narcissist, but playing her was liberating. Therapeutic, even. When she goes jogging in lingerie, we filmed it in this village cul de sac. I trotted around in my bra and knickers while this local woman was out walking her little dog. She kept making rude remarks about me via the dog: “We don’t like that lady, do we?” We shot other scenes in Steve Coogan’s house. When Jill and Glen are in bed, that was Steve’s bed. He was rarely there, so we didn’t bother washing the sheets afterwards.

I did ballet until 14 and secretly wanted to be a dancer, hence Jill dancing a lot. I even had lessons from a pole-dancer. I’m surprised we got permission to ride a horse into church for Terry’s funeral but I fibbed that I was an experienced rider. I was scared it would start rearing up. Luckily it was fine, then I dismounted and did a dance to Alone by Heart. Soft rock suited Jill’s cartoonish flamboyance.
I wanted the theme tune to be Rain by the Cult but Steve suggested this jaunty Ennio Morricone piece. I was a bit resistant but it’s weirdly uplifting. A counterpoint to the horror.

Nighty Night divided people. Some would tell me it was sick or offensive. Others found it funny, which reassured me that we struck the right balance. I just thought it was ridiculously silly. I didn’t realise it had become a cult show until much later. Just recently, a guy stopped his bike to tell me he uses Nighty Night to test out new boyfriends and see if the relationship is going to work. I’d heard about gay clubs doing dress-up nights, so finally went along to one last month. Me and Mark judged the annual Miss Jill Tyrell contest at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern. Incredible.

Apparently Kylie watched the show while going through cancer treatment and loved it. I found that very moving. Cancer has touched my life, too. Nighty Night is me finding a way to deal with that terrifying thing. When George Michael was in a coma with pneumonia, he came round talking in a West Country accent. Turned out he’d been obsessed with Nighty Night and often did Jill impressions. It’s unbelievable it had gone into the recesses of his mind. I put Faith in the opening scene of [twisted romcom] Sally4Ever as a little tribute, hoping he was listening up there.
We still talk about doing another series. Jill might be working in cosmetic surgery nowadays, botching ops. Maybe she’s a mother too, which is a scary thought.

Rebecca Front, actor I did an episode of I’m Alan Partridge with Julia and we hit it off. Suddenly these scripts arrived. I made the mistake of reading the first two episodes and knew I had to do it. It meant cancelling a family holiday, which didn’t go down well.

I based my character Cath on these nice suburban mums from my childhood. Absolutely lovely but with a steely edge. Her passive aggression contrasts with Jill’s chaos. Her lines still get quoted back at me: “Let’s settle up now or it’ll just get nasty” when splitting the bill or “I don’t like it, Cath” when opening a present. Deep down, we all want to be more Jill. “Hiya Cath!” became a catchphrase. Fight attendants often say it as they hand me a drink. “Hiya Cath! Can I have a selfie?”

title_en: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop
excerpt_en: Some major regional players were missing, but the inaugural Asian edition showed it has the potential to be a powerful global platform for Asian pop.
body_en: On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia.

Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia.
The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices.

Regional flavour Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together).

While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English.
By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual.

Musically, it was a diverse offering. The delicate lotus leaves of Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên and her back-up dancers broke into a high-energy opening number, Em Tiên. Malaysia’s Aina Abdul finished the show with a pitch-perfect power ballad, Bluest Sky.
In between, audiences were treated to Cambodian and Bhutanese ballads, Bengali a capella, South Korean K-pop and, perhaps most surprisingly, Nepali rock.

Girls to the front But it was the Philippines’ Carmelle – the youngest contestant, at 19 – who won the night with Sobra-Sobra. The focus of the empowering pop song in English and Tagalog was about Filipino women’s right to be who they want to be.
“It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are. It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas,” Carmelle told The Guardian.
Carmelle received 211 points, winning both the jury and the public vote, encompassing viewers from 183 countries and territories.
With her victory, the Philippines has won the right to host Eurovision Asia in 2027. In the meantime, Carmelle will also perform at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria.

Carmelle rehearsing Sobra-Sobra at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia. Eurovision Song Contest Asia Spectacle and snags Eurovision is known for its spectacle, and Eurovision Asia delivered, albeit on a more modest budget. Stage production made the most of stunning visual projections, smoke and flares.
Eurovision is also known for its non-political stance, with political or ideological messages prohibited.

But it has been more forgiving toward humanitarian statements. And at Eurovision Asia, Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai used the end of his set to call for support for his country as it recovers from the August flood disaster.

The show was not without its hitches. Laos’ representative, Thinla, couldn’t hear her music due to an issue with her earpiece, so footage of her technical rehearsal was shown at the end of the performances to ensure fair judgement of her act.
Thai artists Mang x Daou experienced wardrobe malfunctions during their ballad Aroma, though this didn’t affect their chances in the voting – Thailand came in second place, with 169 points.
Why not Asiavision? If Europe has Eurovision, why can’t Asia have Asiavision?
For one, the name “Asiavision” is already taken: it’s the broadcasting network of the Asia-Pacific Broadcasting Union (ABU), which has its own song contests and festivals.

But mostly, it’s about branding. Although the name Eurovision has become synonymous with the song contest, it actually refers to the European Broadcasting Union’s (EBU) pan-European telecommunications network.
The Eurovision Song Contest was created in 1956 to promote the network and attract audiences across borders. (No, it was not created to unite a war-torn Europe.)

The purpose of Eurovision Asia is specifically to expand the Eurovision brand and format into the region. This is a project the EBU has been attempting for more than two decades. It plans to continue the expansion of the brand through other continental editions.

title_en: Starwatch: Fleeting brilliance of Leonid meteor shower to hit peak
excerpt_en: Annual display appears to radiate from constellation of Leo in eastern sky as Earth passes through comet debris stream
body_en: The annual Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak this week, offering a chance to count meteors. The shower is expected to be at its most active during the night of 17–18 November. Under ideal conditions, observers may see up to 10–15 meteors an hour.
What they lack in numbers, they make up for in brilliance.

The Leonids are produced by dust shed by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the Sun every 33 years. As Earth passes through this debris stream, the particles strike our atmosphere at about 71 km/s, making them among the fastest meteors of any annual shower. As a result, they often leave bright, fleeting streaks across the sky.
The meteors appear to radiate from the constellation of Leo, the lion, which rises in the east after midnight. The chart shows the view looking east from London at midnight on 17–18 November.
Conditions will improve towards dawn as Leo climbs higher in the sky. As an added reward for your efforts, Mars and Jupiter will form a beautiful pair just in front of Leo’s chest.
From the southern hemisphere, Leo remains relatively low in the northern sky, making the hours before dawn the best time to look for meteors.

title_en: Why do blind people and musicians hear pitch better? New research suggests they have less internal noise
excerpt_en: The brain’s ability to process sound more consistently may influence how well you’re able to discriminate between different sounds.
body_en: People who have lived most of their lives blind often have extraordinary hearing abilities. In new research published in the Journal of Neuroscience, my colleagues and I discovered that this ability arises from how their auditory systems are able to more consistently and reliably process sounds compared with people who aren’t blind. And interestingly, sighted musicians seem to enhance their hearing through a similar mechanism.
Hearing is a complicated process. It involves many stages, starting from how the ears detect sounds and going all the way up to how the brain extracts meaningful information from those sounds.

Different mechanisms are involved, too. You can get better at hearing by being more selective or more consistent. Think of writing the letter “A.” You can practice to make your “A” either more distinguishable from “B” or look more similar to other “A’s” every time you write it. The latter is called internal noise – how consistently your auditory system responds to the same sound over time. The less internal noise you have, the more reliably you can tell similar sounds apart.

How does your brain pick out the voice of someone you know from the crowd? Seth Joel/DigitalVision via Getty Images We recruited nine individuals who became blind before the age of 2 and 18 sighted individuals. Participants in both groups had varying levels of musical training, giving us an opportunity to examine how musical experience can also affect hearing abilities.

Participants completed two simple hearing tasks. In one task, they detected a tone presented in background noise, which allowed us to assess how the cochlea in the inner ear processes different sound frequencies. In the other task, they judged which of the two tones had a higher pitch, a task that also relies on how the brain interprets sound information.

We found that people with early-life blindness were better than sighted people only in the pitch discrimination task. This means that their improved hearing abilities may selectively originate from changes in how their brains process auditory information and not from how their ears detect sounds.

Importantly, we used a mathematical model to better understand what drives differences in pitch discrimination. The model showed that the enhanced ability to tell pitches apart in people with early-life blindness happens by reducing internal noise: more consistent and reliable processing of sounds rather than greater selectivity for different sound frequencies.

Surprisingly, we found that musical training seems to similarly reduce internal noise. Sighted musicians also responded to sounds more consistently compared with people who neither experienced early-life blindness nor received extensive musical training.

Why it matters Because your brain doesn’t know what kind of sensory environment it’ll encounter when you’re born, it’s equipped with a special ability: to tune its responses to parts of the world that matter to it.

This ability helps people see, hear and master new skills as their experiences change, like when children learn to read and when adults learn to identify different bird species. Words and birds have become a meaningful part of their experiences, so their brains are tuned to the new information.

Our study identifies internal noise as an important factor that facilitates this brain plasticity. There are many ways a person can come to have reduced levels of internal noise, and one is by building a more accurate template for perceiving the world.
It is possible that sensory experience, whether it be being blind or being a musician, might help create and fine-tune the perceptual template relevant for hearing.

People with musical training also process sound more consistently than people without training. Jose Luis Pelaez Inc/DigitalVision via Getty Images What still isn’t known If sensory experiences and training can tap into the brain’s ability to adapt, researchers may be able to use them to improve perceptual abilities. For example, targeted training to hear sound locations could help people who are beginning to lose vision learn to rely on other senses to navigate.
However, researchers still don’t know how much training is needed and what aspects of the auditory experience are key to drive behaviorally meaningful changes in the brain.

Another important question is whether and how this brain plasticity varies depending on when someone loses their vision or begins musical training. The brain might have greater plasticity early in development, and how sensory experiences shape the brain may differ in adulthood.

What’s next How far can people push their ability to learn? Can everyone become super listeners with training? If the brain’s plasticity is limited in adulthood, are there ways to reopen the door? And what role does internal noise play in this learning?

Moving forward, our team is interested in understanding whether the enhanced pitch discrimination we saw in people with early-life blindness and sighted musicians extends to more complex, everyday listening.
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work.
Woon Ju Park receives funding from NIH and the Georgia Institute of Technology Smithgall-Watts Early Career Award.

title_en: Young men and Latino voters helped drive the Democrats’ blue wave. Why did they abandon Trump?
excerpt_en: Economic issues are almost always front of mind for voters, political scientist Charles Hunt says.
body_en: The young men and Hispanic and Latino voters who helped propel Donald Trump to his presidential victory in 2024 swung sharply towards the Democrats in the midterm elections, contributing to the historic defeat for Republicans.

Charles Hunt, an associate professor of political science at Boise State University in Idaho, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast that the results suggest weakened support for Trump and his MAGA movement among these key groups of voters.

Hispanic and Latino voters “swung heavily towards Trump in 2024”, Hunt says. But midterm results in Florida, Texas and elsewhere “are showing these voters just slingshotting completely in the other direction,” he explains, citing early exit polls and analysis by The New York Times.

Not just back towards where they were in, say, 2018 or 2020 in terms of support for Democrats, but past that – being more supportive of folks like James Talarico in Texas than they have been of any Democrat in the last 20 years.
That’s really, really significant, especially since that’s a growing part of the electorate.

The New York Times’ analysis of voting trends reveals young voters swung back toward the Democratic Party by more than 30 percentage points – the largest shift of any age group. Young men, in particular, swung strongly back towards the Democrats.
The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of voters across all 50 states, shows Democrats regaining ground among young and Hispanic voters, too.

The scale of the Republicans’ defeat goes beyond the usual midterm backlash against a sitting president, Hunt says. He draws a comparison with the 1974 midterm elections following the Watergate scandal and then-President Richard Nixon’s resignation:
This is a level of […] midterm blowback against an incumbent president of the sort that we haven’t seen since 1974. […] It’s really pretty historic and in a completely different league than 2018.
So what drove voters towards the Democrats?
Economic pressures are one reason, Hunt says. He points to the effects of the Iran war and tariffs, particularly on highly visible costs such as petrol:
A lot of political science tells us that economic issues are almost always front of mind for voters.
But those pressures also gave force to Democratic messaging about corruption and an economy favouring billionaires. He adds:

I think those issues tie together with a lot of Democratic messaging around things like corruption, and the influence of billionaires, and Elon Musk spending half a billion dollars in this election probably did not help, at the end of the day.
